goals: Label the principal axis, optical centre, principal foci and focal length of a lens
Explain converging and diverging action using the lens-as-prisms model
Draw ray diagrams for a convex lens for six object positions and describe each image
Explain why a concave lens always forms a virtual, erect, diminished image

slides.heading: Lenses all around us
slides.body_md: Part 1 — a lens is a piece of transparent material bounded by two surfaces, at least one of them curved. Lenses in spectacles, cameras and projectors all work by refraction.

rows: Spread light so distant objects are clear
Form a real image on the sensor

visual.alt: Table of four everyday devices, the kind of lens each uses and its job

slides.narration: Namaste! Your grandmother’s reading glasses, a classmate’s spectacles, the camera in a mobile phone and the peephole in a door all contain lenses. A lens is a piece of glass or plastic with at least one curved surface. In this part we learn how lenses bend light and what kind of image each kind of lens forms.

slides.heading: Convex and concave lenses
slides.body_md: A **convex (converging) lens** is **thicker at the middle** than at the edges; it bends a parallel beam to meet at a point. A **concave (diverging) lens** is **thinner at the middle**; it spreads a parallel beam out. Common shapes: **biconvex**, **plano-convex**, **concavo-convex** (thicker middle); **biconcave**, **plano-concave**, **convexo-concave** (thinner middle). A lens can be pictured as a set of **prisms**: in a convex lens their bases point towards the axis, so all rays bend towards the axis.

slides.narration: A convex lens is thicker in the middle than at its edges, and a concave lens is thinner in the middle. One way to see what they do is to imagine each lens as a stack of small prisms. A prism bends light towards its base. In a convex lens the bases face the axis, so light converges; in a concave lens they face outwards, so light spreads.

slides.heading: Terms used for a lens
slides.body_md:
- **Centres of curvature** $C_{1}$, $C_{2}$: centres of the spheres of which the lens surfaces are parts.
- **Principal axis:** the line through both centres of curvature.
- **Optical centre O:** the point on the axis through which a ray passes **undeviated**.
- **Principal foci $F_{1}$, $F_{2}$:** rays parallel to the axis converge to $F_{2}$ (convex) or appear to diverge from $F_{1}$ (concave); a lens has two foci, one on each side.
- **Focal plane:** the plane through a focus, normal to the axis.
- **Focal length f:** distance from O to a principal focus.

slides.narration: The principal axis passes through the centres of curvature of both lens surfaces. Its midpoint in a thin lens is the optical centre, where light passes straight through. A beam parallel to the axis meets at the principal focus of a convex lens, or seems to come from the principal focus of a concave lens. The distance from the optical centre to the focus is the focal length.

slides.body_md: Identify a converging lens from its shape or action.
slides.narration: Quick check. A converging lens is thicker at the middle than at the edges.

slides.heading: The three principal rays
slides.body_md:
To locate an image, draw any **two** of these rays from the top of the object:
1. A ray **parallel to the principal axis** passes, after refraction, **through $F_{2}$** (convex) or appears to come **from $F_{1}$** (concave).
2. A ray **through the optical centre** goes on **undeviated**.
3. A ray **through $F_{1}$** (convex), or directed towards $F_{2}$ (concave), emerges **parallel to the principal axis**.

Where the refracted rays **meet**, the image is **real**; where they only **appear to meet** when produced backwards, it is **virtual**.

visual.alt: Flow pairing each principal ray before the lens with its path after refraction

slides.narration: Three rays are easy to draw. A ray parallel to the axis bends to pass through the second focus. A ray through the optical centre goes straight on. A ray through the first focus comes out parallel to the axis. Any two of them fix the top of the image. If the rays really meet, the image is real; if they only seem to meet, it is virtual.

slides.heading: Convex lens: object beyond 2F
slides.body_md: Object **beyond 2F₁**: image **between F₂ and 2F₂**, **real, inverted, diminished**. (Used in a **camera** and in the eye.) As the object moves in from infinity towards 2F₁, the image moves out from F₂ towards 2F₂ and grows. For an object **at infinity**, the image is a point-sized, real, inverted image **at F₂**.

slides.narration: When the object is at twice the focal length, the image forms at twice the focal length on the other side. It is real and inverted, and exactly the same size as the object. In the laboratory, finding this position is an easy way to measure the focal length of a convex lens.

slides.heading: Worked example: focal length from a distant tower
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** Meena holds a convex lens so that a sharp image of a distant mobile tower falls on a card 16 cm behind the lens. (a) What is the focal length? (b) Where must she place a candle to get an image of the same size on a screen? (c) How far from the lens will that screen be?

**(a)** Rays from a very distant object are parallel, so the image is at $F_{2}$: $f = 16$ cm.

**(b)** At $2F_{1}$: $2f = 2 \times 16 = 32$ cm in front of the lens.

**(c)** The image is at $2F_{2}$: $32$ cm behind the lens; real, inverted, same size.

visual.alt: Table of object and image positions for the lens of focal length sixteen centimetres

slides.narration: Light from a faraway tower arrives as a parallel beam, so its image forms at the focus. The card is sixteen centimetres away, so that is the focal length. For a same size image, the candle must be at twice the focal length, thirty two centimetres in front, and the sharp image appears thirty two centimetres behind the lens.

slides.heading: Worked example: choosing the object position
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A convex lens has focal length 12 cm. Where should an object be placed to get (a) a real image of the same size, (b) a real, magnified image, (c) an erect, magnified image, (d) a real, diminished image?

**(a)** At $2F_{1}$: $2 \times 12 = 24$ cm from the lens.

**(b)** Between $F_{1}$ and $2F_{1}$: between 12 cm and 24 cm.

**(c)** Between O and $F_{1}$: less than 12 cm (magnifying glass).

**(d)** Beyond $2F_{1}$: more than 24 cm from the lens.

For a bigger real image, place it between twelve and twenty four. For an upright, magnified image, bring it within twelve centimetres. For a smaller real image, move it beyond twenty four.

So, **wherever the object is**, the image is **virtual, erect and diminished**, lying between the focus and the optical centre. (Object at infinity: image at $F_{1}$, highly diminished.)

slides.heading: Summary: Part 1
bullets: Convex lens: thick middle, converging; concave lens: thin middle, diverging (lens as prisms).
Principal rays: parallel → through F₂; through O → undeviated; through F₁ → parallel.
Convex: object beyond 2F → diminished real image; at 2F → same size at 2F; between F and 2F → magnified real beyond 2F; at F → image at infinity.

Concave: always virtual, erect, diminished, between F₁ and O.

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 1. A convex lens converges light and a concave lens diverges it. Two principal rays are enough to locate an image. As an object comes closer to a convex lens, its real image moves away and grows, until inside the focus the image becomes virtual, upright and magnified. A concave lens always gives a small, upright, virtual image.

slides.body_md: Part 2 — ray diagrams tell us roughly where an image is; the **lens formula** tells us exactly. Opticians describe lenses by their **power** in dioptres.

rows: How big is it, and which way up?
How strongly does the lens bend light?

slides.narration: In this part we put numbers on lenses. The lens formula gives the exact position of an image. Magnification tells us its size and whether it is upright. The power of a lens, measured in dioptres, tells an optician how strongly it bends light. First, we need a rule for the signs of distances.

slides.heading: The New Cartesian sign convention
slides.body_md:
1. All distances are measured from the **optical centre O**.
2. Distances measured **in the direction of the incident light** (left to right) are **positive**; those **against** it are **negative**. So a real object has **u negative**.
3. Heights **above** the principal axis are **positive**; **below**, **negative**.

Consequences: $f$ is **positive** for a convex lens and **negative** for a concave lens; a real image (other side) has **v positive**, a virtual image (same side) has **v negative**.

slides.narration: We use the New Cartesian sign convention. Measure every distance from the optical centre. With light travelling from left to right, distances to the right are positive and distances to the left are negative, so the object distance is negative. Heights above the axis are positive. A convex lens has a positive focal length and a concave lens a negative one.

slides.heading: Lens formula and magnification
slides.body_md:
For a thin lens, with all distances in the same unit and signs from the convention:
$$\frac{1}{v} - \frac{1}{u} = \frac{1}{f}$$
**Linear magnification:**
$$m = \frac{h_{2}}{h_{1}} = \frac{v}{u}$$
$m$ **negative** → real, inverted image; $m$ **positive** → virtual, erect image. $|m| > 1$ magnified; $|m| < 1$ diminished.

rows: Real, inverted, other side of lens
Virtual, erect, same side as object

visual.alt: Table linking the signs of image distance and magnification to the nature of the image

slides.narration: The lens formula says one over the image distance, minus one over the object distance, equals one over the focal length. Magnification is image height divided by object height, which also equals image distance divided by object distance. A negative magnification means a real, inverted image; a positive one means a virtual, upright image.

slides.heading: Worked example: a convex lens forming a real image
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A 4.0 cm tall object stands 25 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the position, size and nature of the image.

**Given:** $u = -25$ cm, $f = +15$ cm, $h_{1} = +4.0$ cm.

**Lens formula:** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{25} = \dfrac{5 - 3}{75} = \dfrac{2}{75}$, so $v = +37.5$ cm.

**Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{37.5}{-25} = -1.5$; $h_{2} = m h_{1} = -1.5 \times 4.0 = -6.0$ cm.

**Image:** 37.5 cm behind the lens, real, inverted, 6.0 cm tall (magnified).

visual.alt: Table of the values in the convex lens example

slides.narration: Write the object distance as minus twenty five and the focal length as plus fifteen. One over v equals one fifteenth minus one twenty fifth, which is two seventy-fifths, so v is plus thirty seven and a half centimetres. The magnification is v over u, minus one and a half. So the image is real, upside down and six centimetres tall.

slides.heading: Quick check: using the lens formula
slides.body_md: Find an image distance with the lens formula.
slides.narration: Quick check. Put u in with a negative sign before you calculate.

slides.heading: Worked example: a concave lens
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** An object is placed 30 cm from a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Find the image distance and the magnification.

**Given:** $u = -30$ cm, $f = -15$ cm.

**Lens formula:** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{3}{30}$, so $v = -10$ cm.

**Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-10}{-30} = 0.333$.

**Image:** 10 cm from the lens on the **same side** as the object; virtual, erect, one third the size.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the concave lens example

slides.narration: For a concave lens the focal length is negative, minus fifteen. One over v equals minus one fifteenth minus one thirtieth, which is minus three thirtieths, so v is minus ten centimetres. The minus sign tells us the image is on the same side as the object, so it is virtual. The magnification is one third: upright and smaller.

slides.heading: The magnifying glass
slides.body_md: A **simple microscope** (magnifying glass) is a convex lens of **short focal length**. The object is placed **between O and F**, and the eye sees a **virtual, erect, magnified** image, usually at the least distance of distinct vision (about 25 cm) or farther. A shorter focal length gives a larger image. Uses: reading small print, watch repairing, examining stamps, leaves and insects, palmistry.

slides.narration: A magnifying glass is simply a convex lens with a short focal length, held so that the object is closer to it than its focus. The eye then sees an upright, enlarged, virtual image on the same side as the object. Watch repairers, stamp collectors and biology students all use one to see fine details.

slides.heading: Worked example: a stamp under a magnifying glass
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** A stamp 2.0 cm wide is held 8.0 cm from a magnifying glass of focal length 10 cm. Find where the image is and how wide it appears.

**Lens formula:** $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{10} - \dfrac{1}{8} = \dfrac{4 - 5}{40} = -\dfrac{1}{40}$, so $v = -40$ cm.

**Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-40}{-8} = 5$; image width $= 5 \times 2.0 = 10$ cm.

**Image:** 40 cm from the lens on the stamp’s side; virtual, erect, five times wider.

visual.alt: Table of the values in the magnifying glass example

slides.narration: The stamp is eight centimetres from a lens of focal length ten, so it is inside the focus. One over v equals one tenth minus one eighth, which is minus one fortieth, so v is minus forty centimetres. The magnification is five, positive, so the image is upright, virtual and five times wider: ten centimetres.

slides.heading: Quick check: sign of the focal length
slides.body_md: Apply the sign convention to a lens.
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember which kind of lens has its principal focus on the incident side.

slides.heading: Power of a lens
slides.body_md:
The **power** of a lens is a measure of how strongly it converges or diverges light. It is the **reciprocal of the focal length in metres**:
$$P = \frac{1}{f\ (\text{in m})} = \frac{100}{f\ (\text{in cm})}$$
SI unit: **dioptre (D)**. One dioptre is the power of a lens of focal length **1 m**. Power is **positive for a convex lens** and **negative for a concave lens**. A **shorter focal length** means a **greater power**.

visual.alt: Table of focal lengths and powers of four lenses

slides.narration: Opticians describe a lens by its power, which is one divided by its focal length in metres. The unit is the dioptre. A convex lens of focal length half a metre has a power of plus two dioptres; a concave lens of focal length a quarter of a metre has a power of minus four. The shorter the focal length, the stronger the lens.

slides.heading: Worked example: reading a spectacle prescription
slides.body_md:
**Problem.** (a) A prescription reads $+2.5$ D. What lens is it, and what is its focal length? (b) A camera lens has focal length 40 mm. Find its power.

**(a)** Positive power, so a **convex** lens: $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{2.5} = 0.4$ m $= 40$ cm.

**(b)** $f = 40\ \text{mm} = 0.04$ m; $P = \dfrac{1}{0.04} = 25$ D (convex, very strong).

visual.alt: Table of power and focal length for the spectacle lens and the camera lens

slides.narration: A prescription of plus two and a half dioptres is a convex lens. Its focal length is one divided by two and a half, which is point four metres, or forty centimetres. A camera lens of focal length forty millimetres is point zero four metres, so its power is one divided by that, twenty five dioptres. Always change to metres first.

slides.heading: Quick check: power in dioptres
slides.body_md: Find the power of a lens from its focal length.
slides.narration: Quick check. Change the focal length to metres before you take the reciprocal.

slides.heading: Uses of lenses
slides.body_md:
- **Convex lens:** magnifying glass; camera and projector lens; objective and eyepiece of microscopes and telescopes; spectacles for **long sight (hypermetropia)** and old age; eye lens; making a parallel beam from a lamp at the focus.
- **Concave lens:** spectacles for **short sight (myopia)**; door peephole (wide view); in combination with convex lenses in cameras and binoculars to improve images.

visual.alt: Table of four uses of lenses with the lens and the reason

slides.narration: Convex lenses are used in magnifying glasses, cameras, projectors, microscopes and telescopes, and in spectacles for people who cannot see near things clearly. Concave lenses are used in spectacles for short sight and in door peepholes, and they are combined with convex lenses in good cameras and binoculars.

slides.heading: Summary: Part 2
bullets: Sign convention: distances from O; along the light positive; u is negative for a real object; f + for convex, − for concave.
Magnification m = h₂/h₁ = v/u; negative → real, inverted; positive → virtual, erect.
Power P = 1/f (f in m), unit dioptre; + convex, − concave.
Magnifying glass: convex lens of short focal length, object within F, virtual erect magnified image.

visual.alt: Summary table of the three formulae of Part 2

slides.narration: Let us sum up Part 2. Use the sign convention: the object distance is negative, the focal length of a convex lens positive and of a concave lens negative. The lens formula gives the image distance, and magnification is image distance over object distance. Power is one over the focal length in metres, measured in dioptres.

sections.heading: 1. Lenses and their terms
sections.body_md:
- **Lens:** a transparent medium bounded by two surfaces, at least one curved (usually spherical).
- **Convex (converging):** thicker at the middle — biconvex, plano-convex, concavo-convex. **Concave (diverging):** thinner at the middle — biconcave, plano-concave, convexo-concave.
- **Lens as prisms:** a convex lens behaves like prisms with bases towards the axis (light bends towards the axis); a concave lens like prisms with apexes towards the axis (light bends away).
- **Centres of curvature, principal axis, optical centre O** (ray through it is undeviated), **principal foci F₁ and F₂**, **focal plane** (plane through F normal to the axis), **focal length f** (distance OF).
- A lens has two principal foci, one on each side; for a thin lens in air both focal lengths are equal.

key_terms.definition_md: The point on the principal axis of a lens through which a ray of light passes without deviation.
The point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after refraction.
The distance between the optical centre and a principal focus of a lens.

sections.heading: 2. Images formed by a convex lens
sections.body_md:
**Principal rays:** (1) parallel to the axis → through F₂; (2) through O → undeviated; (3) through F₁ → parallel to the axis. Two rays fix the image; real where rays meet, virtual where they appear to meet.

| Object position | Image position | Nature and size | Use |
|---|---|---|---|
| At infinity | At F₂ | Real, inverted, highly diminished | Burning glass, telescope objective |
| Beyond 2F₁ | Between F₂ and 2F₂ | Real, inverted, diminished | Camera |
| At 2F₁ | At 2F₂ | Real, inverted, same size | Photocopier |
| Between F₁ and 2F₁ | Beyond 2F₂ | Real, inverted, magnified | Projector |
| At F₁ | At infinity | Real, inverted, highly magnified | Searchlight beam |
| Between O and F₁ | Same side, beyond the object | Virtual, erect, magnified | Magnifying glass |

An image formed where refracted rays only appear to meet when produced backwards; it cannot be caught on a screen.

sections.heading: 3. Images formed by a concave lens
sections.body_md:
- Ray parallel to the axis diverges as if from F₁; ray through O goes straight on.
- The refracted rays never meet; produced back, they meet **between F₁ and O**.
- For **every** position of a real object the image is **virtual, erect, diminished**, between F₁ and O, on the object side. For an object at infinity the image is at F₁, highly diminished.
- A quick test: a lens that always gives a smaller, upright image of objects at all distances is concave.

key_terms.definition_md: A lens that spreads a parallel beam so that the rays appear to come from its principal focus; a concave lens.

rows: At F₁, highly diminished, virtual, erect

sections.heading: 4. Sign convention, lens formula and magnification
sections.body_md:
**New Cartesian sign convention:** distances from O; along the incident light (left to right) positive, against it negative; heights up positive, down negative. Hence $u < 0$ for a real object; $f > 0$ convex, $f < 0$ concave; $v > 0$ real image, $v < 0$ virtual image.

**Lens formula:** $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$. **Magnification:** $m = \dfrac{h_{2}}{h_{1}} = \dfrac{v}{u}$ — negative for real, inverted images; positive for virtual, erect ones.

Method: list $u$, $v$, $f$ with signs → substitute → solve → interpret the signs.

key_terms.definition_md: The ratio of the height of the image to the height of the object, equal to v divided by u for a lens.

sections.heading: 5. Power of a lens; magnifying glass; uses
sections.body_md:
- **Power** $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$ with $f$ in metres; unit **dioptre (D)**; $1\ \text{D}$ is the power of a lens of focal length 1 m. Convex: $P > 0$; concave: $P < 0$.
- **Magnifying glass (simple microscope):** convex lens of short focal length; object between O and F; image virtual, erect, magnified, usually at about 25 cm from the eye. Shorter focal length → greater magnification.
- **Uses:** convex — magnifying glass, camera, projector, microscope and telescope lenses, spectacles for long sight; concave — spectacles for short sight, peephole, lens combinations.

key_terms.definition_md: The reciprocal of the focal length of a lens expressed in metres; it measures the converging or diverging ability of the lens.
The power of a lens whose focal length is one metre.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Taking u as positive for a real object.
- Forgetting that f is negative for a concave lens.
- Using f in cm to calculate power (power needs metres).
- Drawing virtual rays or images with full lines; missing arrows on rays.
- Calling the magnifying-glass image “real”.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- Ray diagrams: two correct rays with arrows (1), image correctly placed and labelled (1).
- Numericals: signed data and formula (1), substitution (1), answer with unit and interpretation (1).
- Nature of image: real or virtual, erect or inverted, magnified or diminished — all three words.

questions.stem_md: Sunil wants to focus the parallel rays of sunlight to a bright spot on a dry leaf. He should use a lens that is:

options.text_md: thinner at its centre than at its edges
flat on both faces
curved inwards on one face and flat on the other
thicker at its centre than at its edges

questions.solution_md: A lens thicker at the middle is convex, a converging lens — option (d).

questions.stem_md: When a concave lens is pictured as a set of small prisms, the prisms:

options.text_md: have their apexes towards the principal axis, so rays bend away from the axis
have their bases towards the principal axis, so rays bend towards the axis
are all identical, so rays are not bent
have their bases towards the axis, so rays bend away from it

questions.solution_md: A prism bends light towards its base; in a concave lens the bases point outwards, so light diverges — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Through which point of a thin lens does a ray of light pass without any deviation?

options.text_md: The principal focus
The centre of curvature of one surface
Any point on the rim
The optical centre

questions.solution_md: Near the optical centre the faces are parallel, like a thin slab — option (d).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A thin lens in air has two principal foci, one on each side, at equal distances from its optical centre.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: F₁ and F₂ lie at the same distance f on either side.

questions.stem_md: The plane passing through the principal focus of a lens, normal to the principal axis, is called the ___ plane.
questions.solution_md: **Focal** plane.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A convex lens is called a converging lens.

**Reason (R):** It behaves like a set of prisms with their bases towards the principal axis, so it bends rays towards the axis.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: On a sunny day, a convex lens can be used to burn a hole in a sheet of paper, but a concave lens cannot. Explain why.

answer.model_answer_md: Sunlight arrives as a parallel beam. The convex lens converges this beam to its principal focus, concentrating the energy at one small spot that becomes hot enough to burn the paper. A concave lens spreads the beam out, so the light is never concentrated.

questions.solution_md: Converges to focus vs diverges.

marking_scheme.step: Convex lens converges the parallel beam at its focus

questions.stem_md: Priya is given two lenses that look alike from a distance. Without touching their surfaces, how can she find out which one is convex? Give a reason.

answer.model_answer_md: She can hold each lens close to printed text and look through it. The lens that makes the letters look larger and upright is convex (the print lies within its focus, giving a virtual magnified image); the one that makes them look smaller is concave.

questions.solution_md: Look at print; convex magnifies.

questions.stem_md: In a slide projector, the slide is 18 cm from a convex lens of focal length 12 cm. The image on the screen is:

options.text_md: virtual, erect and magnified, 36 cm from the lens
real, inverted and diminished, 20 cm from the lens
real, inverted and the same size, 24 cm from the lens
real, inverted and magnified, 36 cm from the lens

questions.solution_md: The slide is between F and 2F, so the image is beyond 2F: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{18} = \dfrac{1}{36}$, $v = 36$ cm, real, inverted, magnified — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A narrow beam from a laser torch, parallel to the principal axis, falls on a concave lens. After passing through the lens, the rays:

options.text_md: meet at the principal focus on the far side of the lens
spread out as if they were coming from the principal focus on the side of the incident light
stay parallel to the principal axis
all pass through the optical centre

questions.solution_md: A concave lens diverges a parallel beam so that it appears to come from F₁ — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The image formed by a convex lens of an object placed at 2F₁ is the same size as the object.

**Reason (R):** Every image formed by a convex lens is real.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true; R is false — a convex lens gives a virtual image when the object is within F — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A lens of power +4 D has a focal length of 25 cm.

**Reason (R):** A convex lens is thicker at the middle than at its edges.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true ($f = \dfrac{1}{4} = 0.25$ m), but R does not explain A, which follows from $P = \dfrac{1}{f}$ — option (b).

False

questions.solution_md: True: the image is always erect (m positive) and diminished (m less than 1).

options.text_md: at twice the focal length, real, inverted and the same size
just beyond the focus, real, inverted and highly diminished
on the same side as the friend, virtual and erect
at infinity, real and magnified

questions.solution_md: The friend is far beyond 2F, so the image is real, inverted, diminished and lies just beyond F — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A candle placed 30 cm in front of a convex lens gives a sharp image of exactly the same size on a screen. The focal length of the lens is:

60 cm

15 cm

questions.solution_md: Same-size image means object at 2F: $2f = 30$ cm, so $f = 15$ cm — option (d).

options.text_md: at twice the focal length from the lens
between the focus and the lens
at the principal focus of the lens
very far from the lens

questions.solution_md: Rays from a point at F emerge parallel — option (c).

options.text_md: moves away from the lens and becomes larger
moves towards the lens and becomes smaller
stays at 2F₂ but becomes larger
becomes virtual and erect

questions.solution_md: The image moves from 2F₂ towards infinity and grows — option (a).

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: every real image of a real object formed by a single lens is inverted.

questions.solution_md: **Infinity**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A ray of light passing through the first principal focus of a convex lens emerges parallel to the principal axis.

**Reason (R):** A ray parallel to the axis passes through the principal focus, and the path of light is reversible.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Where must a document be placed in front of the convex lens of a copying camera to obtain a copy of the same size?

answer.model_answer_md: At twice the focal length (2F₁) from the lens.

questions.solution_md: At 2F₁.

questions.stem_md: Describe, as you would draw it, how two principal rays locate the image of an object placed beyond 2F₁ of a convex lens. State the nature of the image.

answer.model_answer_md: From the top of the object, draw a ray parallel to the axis that passes through F₂ after refraction, and a ray through the optical centre that goes straight on. They cross between F₂ and 2F₂ below the axis; the image is real, inverted and diminished.

questions.solution_md: Two rays; image between F₂ and 2F₂.

questions.stem_md: A convex lens has a focal length of 8 cm. State the position and nature of the image when an object is placed at (a) 30 cm, (b) 16 cm and (c) 5 cm from the lens.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Beyond 2F₁ (2F = 16 cm): image between F₂ and 2F₂, real, inverted, diminished. (b) At 2F₁: image at 2F₂, 16 cm behind the lens, real, inverted, same size. (c) Within F: image on the same side as the object, virtual, erect, magnified.

questions.solution_md: Diminished real; same size at 2F; virtual magnified.

questions.stem_md: A lamp is 60 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 15 cm. Its image is:

options.text_md: real, inverted and diminished, -12 cm behind the lens
virtual, erect and diminished, -12 cm from the lens on the lamp’s side
virtual, erect and magnified, 20 cm from the lens
real, inverted and the same size, 60 cm behind the lens

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{60} = -\dfrac{5}{60}$, so $v = -12$ cm: virtual, erect, diminished — option (b).

questions.stem_md: Rahul moves a candle from far away steadily towards a concave lens. Its image:

options.text_md: becomes real when the candle passes F₁
becomes larger than the candle once the candle is within F₁
moves from near F₁ towards the lens and grows, but stays smaller than the candle
stays at F₁ and does not change size

questions.solution_md: A concave lens always gives a virtual, erect, diminished image between F₁ and O; it approaches O and grows towards object size — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? Bringing a lit candle very close to a diverging lens makes the lens produce an image of the flame that can be caught on a screen.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: the refracted rays always diverge, so the image of a real object is always virtual.

questions.stem_md: The image formed by a concave lens always lies between its principal focus and its ___ centre.
questions.solution_md: **Optical** centre.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A distant tree seen through a concave lens looks upright and smaller.

**Reason (R):** A concave lens makes rays diverge so that they appear to come from a point between F₁ and the lens.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Rohit claims that if he moves a pencil close enough to a diverging lens, he can catch its image on a screen. Explain why he is wrong, and state where the image always lies.

answer.model_answer_md: A concave lens bends every ray away from the principal axis, so the refracted rays from a point of the object always spread apart and never actually meet. They only appear to meet when produced backwards, on the object side, between the principal focus F₁ and the optical centre.

questions.solution_md: Diverging rays; between F₁ and O.

questions.stem_md: Light falls on a diverging lens from the left. Using the New Cartesian convention, its focal length is taken as:

options.text_md: positive, because focal length is a distance
negative, because its image is always inverted
negative, because its principal focus lies on the side of the incident light
zero, because it has no real focus

questions.solution_md: F of a concave lens is on the incident side, against the light, so f < 0 — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A toy car stands 24 cm from a convex lens whose focal length is 8 cm. Where does its image form? (v, with sign)

options.text_md: +12 cm
+6 cm
−12 cm
+16 cm

questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{8} + \dfrac{1}{-24} = \dfrac{3 - 1}{24} = \dfrac{1}{12}$, so $v = +12$ cm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A lens forms an image at v = +45 cm of an object at u = −15 cm. The magnification and the nature of the image are:

options.text_md: m = −3; real, inverted, three times as tall
m = +3; virtual, erect, three times as tall
m = −0.33; real, inverted, diminished
m = +0.33; virtual, erect, diminished

questions.solution_md: $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{45}{-15} = -3$ — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A 6.0 cm tall candle stands 36 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 12 cm. Find the image distance v in cm (with sign).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{36} = \dfrac{2}{36}$, so $v = \dfrac{36}{2} = 18$ cm (real image).

questions.stem_md: For the same 6.0 cm candle 36 cm in front of the convex lens of focal length 12 cm, the image forms 18 cm behind the lens. (a) Calculate the magnification. (b) Find the height of the image. (c) State three characteristics of the image.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{18}{-36} = -0.5$. (b) $h_{2} = m h_{1} = -0.5 \times 6.0 = -3$ cm: 3.0 cm tall, below the axis. (c) Real, inverted and diminished (half the size).

questions.solution_md: −0.5; −3.0 cm; real, inverted, diminished.

questions.stem_md: An object is placed 24 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 12 cm. Find the image distance v in cm (with sign).
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{f} + \dfrac{1}{u} = -\dfrac{1}{12} - \dfrac{1}{24} = -\dfrac{3}{24}$, so $v = -\dfrac{24}{3} = -8$ cm (virtual, on the object side).

questions.stem_md: A lamp is 30 cm in front of a lens, and a sharp image of it is caught on a screen 60 cm behind the lens. Find the focal length of the lens in cm.
A stamp collector holds a convex lens of focal length 15 cm at 10 cm from a stamp. What magnification does the lens produce?
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{10} = \dfrac{2 - 3}{30} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30$ cm; $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-30}{-10} = 3$ (virtual, erect).

questions.stem_md: A convex lens of focal length 20 cm forms a real image three times the size of an object. How far from the lens (in cm) is the object? Give a positive distance.
questions.solution_md: Real image: $m = -3$, so $v = -3u$. Then $\dfrac{1}{-3u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{20}$ gives $-\dfrac{4}{3u} = \dfrac{1}{20}$, so $u = -\dfrac{80}{3} = -26.67$ cm; the object is $\dfrac{80}{3} = 26.7$ cm from the lens.

questions.stem_md: A concave lens of focal length 18 cm forms an image of a toy placed 36 cm in front of it. Find the magnification, to three significant figures.
questions.solution_md: $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{18} - \dfrac{1}{36} = -\dfrac{3}{36}$, so $v = -12$ cm; $m = \dfrac{v}{u} = \dfrac{-12}{-36} = 0.333$ (virtual, erect, diminished).

questions.stem_md: A real object always sits on the incoming-light side of a lens, so in the New Cartesian convention its distance u carries a ___ sign.
questions.solution_md: **Negative**.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A lens gives a magnification of −2 for an object; this image can be caught on a screen.

**Reason (R):** A negative magnification means the image is real and inverted.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md: True or false? If the image distance worked out from the lens formula is negative, the image is virtual and lies on the same side as the object.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: True: negative distances are measured against the incident light, on the object side.

questions.stem_md: Write the lens formula used with the New Cartesian sign convention, naming the symbols.

answer.model_answer_md: 1/v − 1/u = 1/f, where v is the image distance, u the object distance and f the focal length, all from the optical centre.

questions.stem_md: List the rules used to give signs to distances and heights for a lens (New Cartesian convention), and say what sign the focal length of each type of lens takes.

answer.model_answer_md: Distances are measured from the optical centre; those in the direction of the incident light are positive and those against it negative; heights above the axis are positive and below negative. A convex lens has positive f, a concave lens negative f.

questions.solution_md: Rules; f signs.

questions.stem_md: A concave lens has a focal length of 20 cm. Its power is:
questions.solution_md: $P = \dfrac{1}{f} = \dfrac{1}{-0.20} = -5$ D — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A convex lens used in a toy telescope has a focal length of 80 cm. Find its power in dioptres.
An optician’s prescription reads −1.25 D. Find the focal length of the lens in cm (with sign).
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{1}{P} = \dfrac{1}{-1.25} = -0.8$ m, so $f = -0.8 \times 100 = -80$ cm (concave).

questions.stem_md: A lens has a power of +8 D. Find its focal length in cm.
questions.solution_md: $f = \dfrac{100}{P} = \dfrac{100}{8} = 12.5$ cm (convex).

questions.stem_md: A biology student uses a convex lens as a magnifying glass to look at the hairs on a leaf. The leaf must be placed:

options.text_md: exactly at the principal focus
between F and 2F
between the lens and its principal focus
beyond 2F

questions.solution_md: Only within F does a convex lens give a virtual, erect, magnified image — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Two convex lenses have focal lengths of 5 cm and 50 cm. The better one to use as a magnifying glass, and its power, is:

options.text_md: the 5 cm lens, with power +20 D
the 50 cm lens, with power +2 D
the 5 cm lens, with power +0.2 D
the 50 cm lens, with power +50 D

questions.solution_md: A shorter focal length gives a larger image; $P = \dfrac{1}{0.05} = 20$ D — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A lens of focal length 0.5 m has a power of 2 ___.
questions.solution_md: **Dioptres** (D).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A lens of power −3 D is a converging lens.

options.text_md: True
False

questions.solution_md: False: negative power means a diverging (concave) lens.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A convex lens of focal length 10 cm has a greater power than a convex lens of focal length 25 cm.

**Reason (R):** The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true (+10 D against +4 D), and R explains A — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** A magnifying glass forms a real image of a small insect.

**Reason (R):** The insect is held between the lens and its principal focus.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false — the image is virtual and erect; R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A watch repairer wears an eyeglass that is a convex lens of short focal length. (a) Where does he hold the tiny gear relative to the lens? (b) State the nature of the image he sees.

answer.model_answer_md: (a) Closer to the lens than its principal focus (between the optical centre and F). (b) Virtual, erect and magnified, on the same side of the lens as the gear.

questions.solution_md: Within F; virtual, erect, magnified.

questions.stem_md: Name the kind of lens used in the spectacles of a student who cannot see the blackboard clearly from the back of the class.
questions.solution_md: Concave.

questions.stem_md: Match each device in Column A with the lens and object position it uses in Column B.

options.text_md: Slide projector
Magnifying glass
Camera
Door peephole

match_right.text_md: Convex lens, object between F and 2F

questions.solution_md: Projector → between F and 2F; magnifying glass → within F; camera → beyond 2F; peephole → concave lens.

questions.stem_md: Match each quantity in Column A with its correct sign or unit in Column B.

options.text_md: Focal length of a concave lens
Power of a lens
Magnification of a real image
Image distance of a real image

questions.solution_md: Concave f → negative; power → dioptre; real-image m → negative, no unit; real-image v → positive.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Define (i) the optical centre, (ii) the principal focus and (iii) the focal length of a convex lens. [3]

(b) Describe, as you would draw it, the ray diagram for an object placed beyond 2F₁ of a convex lens, and state the position and nature of the image. [3]

(c) For a convex lens, state where the object should be placed to obtain an image that is (i) real and the same size, (ii) virtual and magnified, (iii) at infinity, and (iv) real, magnified, for use in a projector. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) (i) The point on the principal axis through which a ray passes undeviated. (ii) The point on the axis where rays parallel to the axis meet after refraction. (iii) The distance from the optical centre to the principal focus.

(b) A ray from the top of the object parallel to the axis bends through F₂; a ray through O goes straight; a ray through F₁ emerges parallel. They meet between F₂ and 2F₂ below the axis: the image is real, inverted and diminished.

(c) (i) At 2F₁. (ii) Between O and F₁. (iii) At F₁. (iv) Between F₁ and 2F₁.

questions.solution_md: Definitions; ray diagram; four positions.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Explain how signs are given to u, v and f for a lens, and write the lens formula. [3]

(b) A 2.5 cm tall object is placed 20 cm in front of a convex lens of focal length 15 cm. Calculate (i) the image distance, (ii) the magnification and (iii) the height of the image. [3]

(c) The object is moved to 10 cm from the same lens. (i) Find the new image distance. (ii) Find the magnification. (iii) State the nature of the image. (iv) Name a device that uses this arrangement. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Distances from the optical centre; along the incident light positive, against it negative; heights up positive, down negative. Lens formula: $\dfrac{1}{v} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{f}$.

(b) (i) $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{20} = \dfrac{1}{60}$, so $v = +60$ cm. (ii) $m = \dfrac{60}{-20} = -3$. (iii) $h_{2} = -3 \times 2.5 = -7.5$ cm (inverted).

(c) (i) $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{15} - \dfrac{1}{10} = -\dfrac{1}{30}$, so $v = -30$ cm. (ii) $m = \dfrac{-30}{-10} = 3$. (iii) Virtual, erect, magnified, on the object side. (iv) A magnifying glass.

questions.solution_md: Rules and formula; real image; virtual image.

questions.stem_md:
(a) Describe, as you would draw it, the ray diagram for an object placed in front of a concave lens, and state the nature of the image. [3]

(b) An object is placed 30 cm in front of a concave lens of focal length 20 cm. Calculate (i) the image distance and (ii) the magnification, and (iii) state whether the image is magnified or diminished. [3]

(c) (i) Explain why a concave lens cannot form a real image of a real object. (ii) Where does the image lie when the object is very far away? (iii) Give two uses of a concave lens. [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) From the top of the object, a ray parallel to the axis leaves the lens diverging as if from F₁ (drawn dotted back to F₁); a ray through O goes straight on. Produced backwards they meet between F₁ and O on the object side: the image is virtual, erect and diminished.

(b) (i) $\dfrac{1}{v} = -\dfrac{1}{20} - \dfrac{1}{30} = -\dfrac{5}{60}$, so $v = -12$ cm. (ii) $m = \dfrac{-12}{-30} = 0.4$. (iii) Diminished (and erect, virtual).

(c) (i) It always makes the refracted rays diverge, so they never actually meet. (ii) At the principal focus F₁ (highly diminished). (iii) Spectacles for short sight; door peepholes (also in lens combinations).

questions.solution_md: Diagram; image distance and magnification; reasons and uses.

questions.stem_md:
(a) What does the power of a lens measure? Write it in terms of the focal length, name its SI unit, and say how its sign is decided. [3]

(b) Find the power of (i) a convex lens of focal length 20 cm and (ii) a concave lens of focal length 50 cm. (iii) Which lens is stronger? [3]

(c) A magnifying glass of focal length 5.0 cm is held 4.0 cm from a printed letter. (i) Find the image distance. (ii) Find the magnification. (iii) State the nature of the image. (iv) Why is a lens of short focal length preferred? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Power is the reciprocal of the focal length expressed in metres; its SI unit is the dioptre (D), the power of a lens of focal length 1 m. It is positive for a convex lens and negative for a concave lens, following the sign of f.

(b) (i) $P = \dfrac{1}{0.20} = +5$ D. (ii) $P = \dfrac{1}{-0.50} = -2$ D. (iii) The convex lens: its power has the larger magnitude.

(c) (i) $\dfrac{1}{v} = \dfrac{1}{5} - \dfrac{1}{4} = -\dfrac{1}{20}$, so $v = -20$ cm. (ii) $m = \dfrac{-20}{-4} = 5$. (iii) Virtual, erect, magnified, on the same side as the letter. (iv) A shorter focal length (greater power) gives a larger image.

questions.solution_md: Definition; two powers; magnifying glass.

questions.stem_md:
Asha has a convex lens of focal length 15 cm.

(a) She wants a real image twice the size of a bulb on a wall. Find where she must place the bulb and where the wall must be. [3]

(b) She now wants an erect image twice the size of a seed. Find where the seed must be and where the image forms. [3]

(c) (i) Compare the signs of m in (a) and (b), and explain what they tell you. (ii) Could a concave lens give either image? Give a reason. (iii) Which of the two arrangements is used in a projector? [4]

answer.model_answer_md:
(a) Real image: $m = -2$, so $v = -2u$. Then $\dfrac{1}{-2u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15}$ gives $-\dfrac{3}{2u} = \dfrac{1}{15}$, so $u = -22.5$ cm and $v = +45$ cm: bulb 22.5 cm in front of the lens, wall 45 cm behind it.

(b) Erect image: $m = +2$, so $v = 2u$. Then $\dfrac{1}{2u} - \dfrac{1}{u} = \dfrac{1}{15}$ gives $-\dfrac{1}{2u} = \dfrac{1}{15}$, so $u = -7.5$ cm and $v = -15$ cm: seed 7.5 cm from the lens, image 15 cm from the lens on the seed’s side.

(c) (i) In (a) m is negative: real and inverted; in (b) m is positive: virtual and erect. (ii) No: a concave lens always gives a diminished image (and never a real one). (iii) Arrangement (a), with the object between F and 2F.

questions.solution_md: Real ×2; virtual ×2; comparison.
